entries.title: Gravity, the pull between objects
entries.answer: Gravity is a pull between objects that have mass. A ball falls to the floor because Earth pulls it down. The ball pulls back on Earth too, but the ball is so small compared with Earth that you cannot notice the effect. Gravity also helps keep planets in their paths around the Sun. A moving planet would travel away in a straight line without the Sun’s pull. The pull keeps bending the planet’s path, so it curves around the Sun instead.
facts: Gravity gives you weight.
The Moon’s gravity helps cause Earth’s ocean tides.

entries.title: How an electric circuit makes a light work
entries.answer: An electric circuit gives electric charges a path to move along. In a simple flashlight, the battery, bulb, and wires can make a loop. With the switch on, the loop is closed and electric current can flow. The bulb changes some of the electrical energy into light. The switch opens a little gap when you turn it off, and the current stops flowing. A metal wire is a useful part of a circuit because charges move through many metals much more easily than they move through plastic.
facts: Materials that let electric charges move easily are called conductors.
Plastic can help keep current inside the metal wires it covers.

questions.text: What are the forms energy can change into?
How can an electric current create a magnetic field?

entries.title: How can two lights work separately on one battery?
entries.answer: Imagine two lamps connected so each has its own path between the battery’s ends. Electricity can travel in both branches of this parallel circuit. If one branch is opened by a switch, the other still has a complete path, so its lamp can stay lit. Most homes use the same general idea for many devices. Turning off your bedroom lamp need not stop the light across the hallway. A circuit can also use both series and parallel ideas in different places.
facts: Branches connected between the same pair of points have the same voltage across them.

questions.text: What happens to two lamps that share only one path?
How does part of a house’s wiring turn off automatically?
How does power reach all the different branches in a town?

entries.title: How curved lenses bend light
entries.answer: A straw looks bent in water because light from it changes direction when it crosses from water into air at an angle. This is called refraction. A lens uses curved surfaces to bend light in a chosen way. A magnifying glass is thicker in the middle, so it can bring rays of light together. A lens that is thinner in the middle can spread rays out. Different lenses help cameras, microscopes and eyeglasses make clearer pictures.
facts: Light also changes speed when it goes from air into water or glass.

questions.text: What happens when raindrops bend different colors by different amounts?

entries.title: How magnets pull and push
entries.answer: A magnet can pull some materials toward it without touching them. Iron is one example. A magnet has a north end and a south end, called poles. Put the north end of one magnet near the south end of another, and they pull together. Put two north ends near each other, and they push apart. The space around a magnet where it can push or pull has a magnetic field. Electric current can make a magnetic field too. That is one link between electricity and magnets.
facts: A magnet does not pull every metal strongly.
A compass needle turns to line up with Earth’s magnetic field.

How are materials like iron named and grouped?

entries.title: How moving air and water carry heat
entries.answer: When a heater warms nearby air, that air often spreads out and becomes less dense. Cooler, denser air pushes it upward and moves into its place. This can set up a moving loop that carries warmth from one part of a room to another. Water can carry heat in a similar way. Heat transfer by the movement of a gas or liquid is called convection. Fans and pumps can also move warm air or water around.
facts: Convection involves flowing material, while conduction can transfer heat through a solid that stays in place.

entries.title: How sound moves through the air
entries.answer: Sound starts with something moving back and forth. When you pluck a guitar string, it shakes the air nearby. The air pushes on the air next to it, and the pattern spreads outward as a wave. When the wave reaches your ear, it can make your eardrum move. Faster back-and-forth motion can make a higher note. Sound can travel through water and solid objects too. It cannot cross totally empty space because there is no material there to carry the shaking.
facts: An echo is sound that has bounced back to you.
A vibration is motion that repeats back and forth.

Why do you see lightning before you hear thunder?

entries.title: How sunlight warms Earth through empty space
entries.answer: The space between Earth and the Sun is mostly empty, so air cannot carry the Sun’s heat all the way here. Energy travels through space as radiation, including visible light and infrared light. The ground and ocean absorb some of this energy and warm up. Warm things also give off radiation. For instance, near a campfire you can feel warmth on the side of your face that is pointed toward it, even when cooler air is moving past.
facts: Human eyes cannot see infrared light, but special cameras can record it.

entries.title: How wings hold up an airplane
entries.answer: A wing moving through air changes how the air moves over and under its surface. In flight, the wing pushes some air downward. The air pushes the wing upward in return. Air generally presses harder underneath than on top while a wing is making upward lift. The pilot can change speed or the angle of the wing to change this force. For steady, level flight, lift must balance the aircraft’s weight.
facts: In steady, powered flight, thrust balances the backward force of air resistance.

entries.title: Light and the colors we see
entries.answer: Light brings energy from one place to another. The Sun gives off light. So does a light bulb. Most objects around you do not give off their own visible light. You can see a blue notebook because light hits it, and some of the light that bounces back reaches your eyes. The color you see depends on which light reaches you. White light can be a mixture of colors. A glass prism can spread white light out so that you can see the colors separately.
facts: Light can travel through empty space.
Visible light is the part of a much wider family of waves that our eyes can detect.

entries.title: The kinds of light our eyes cannot see
entries.answer: Visible light is only a small part of a large family of waves. At one end, radio waves have much longer spaces between their peaks than visible light. At the other end, ultraviolet light and X-rays have shorter spaces. A radio can detect waves your eyes miss, while a camera made for infrared light can show patterns of warmth. All these waves travel at the same speed in empty space, even though their wavelengths differ.
facts: Visible light ranges in color from red through violet.

entries.title: What energy can do
entries.answer: Energy lets things move or change. A rolling ball has energy because it is moving. A ball you hold above the ground can give up stored energy if you drop it. Energy can also go from one object to another or change form. In a lamp, electrical energy becomes light and heat. A plant uses some of the Sun’s light energy to make sugars. Energy does not come from nothing. When a moving ball slows down and stops, energy has moved into its surroundings, for example as heat or sound.
facts: Energy of motion is called kinetic energy.
Light can carry energy, and moving objects also have energy.

entries.title: What happens when lights share one path?
entries.answer: In a series circuit, the electric current has one path to follow. Imagine a wire from a small battery to a lamp, then to another lamp, then back to the battery. Current runs through both lamps in turn. If one connection opens, it breaks the only path and both lamps go out. A switch put anywhere along that path can turn both lamps off together. A lamp needs a closed path before it can shine.
facts: The same amount of current flows through each part of a single series path.

entries.title: Where an echo comes from
entries.answer: An echo is a sound you hear after it bounces off a surface and returns. At the edge of a canyon, a shout can travel to a cliff and back. Sound takes time to travel, so returning sound from far away arrives after the original shout. Inside a small room, many nearby surfaces reflect sounds so quickly that the returns blend together. Soft walls often absorb more sound than bare hard ones.
facts: A distant echo has to make a two-way trip from the source to the reflecting surface and back.

entries.title: Why a clear daytime sky looks blue
entries.answer: Sunlight contains many colors. As it passes through the atmosphere, tiny molecules of gas send some of its light in new directions. The gas scatters blue light more strongly than red light, sending blue light toward your eyes from many directions. If there were no air to scatter the light, most of the sky away from the Sun would look dark, as it does from the surface of the Moon.
facts: The effect that sends light in different directions is called scattering.

entries.title: Why a push comes with a push back
entries.answer: If you push your hands against a wall, the wall pushes back on your hands just as hard. Every push or pull between two objects works in both directions. On a rolling chair, you can press gently against a wall and move away from it. Your chair moves because wheels make it easier to roll, even though the wall is also receiving a push. A spacecraft can move by pushing gas one way so the gas pushes it the other way.
facts: The two forces in a pair act on different objects, so they do not cancel on one object.

entries.title: Why a spoon handle gets warm
entries.answer: Put a metal spoon in something warm and, after a while, you may feel the handle warm up too. The warm end gives energy to nearby parts of the metal. Energy spreads along the spoon even while the spoon itself stays in place. This kind of heat transfer is called conduction. Wood is much poorer at carrying heat than many metals. That is why cooking tools often have wood or plastic handles.
facts: Heat moves from warmer regions toward cooler regions when they can exchange energy.

entries.title: Why can a rubbed balloon stick to a wall?
entries.answer: Rub a balloon against some fabrics and a few electrons can move from one surface to the other. That leaves one surface with extra negative charge and the other with less. Bringing the balloon close to a wall can shift charges in the wall slightly. The opposite charges are then a little closer to the balloon than the similar charges are. The pull of the closer charges can be strong enough to hold the balloon up for a while.
facts: “Static” describes charge that has collected on a surface instead of flowing steadily in a circuit.

entries.title: Why friction helps us walk
entries.answer: When you step forward, your shoe presses backward on the ground for a moment. Friction is the force between the shoe and ground that helps keep the shoe from sliding. That grip lets the ground push you forward. On slippery ice, there may not be enough friction to get that same push. Friction also slows a book sliding on a desk and lets a pencil leave a mark as its tip rubs across paper.
facts: Friction can act before any sliding takes place.

entries.title: Why mirrors show a clear image
entries.answer: Ordinary walls bounce light in many directions. A smooth mirror sends much of that light in a more orderly way. Each ray bounces out at the same angle it came in, measured from a line sticking straight out of the mirror. Your brain traces the light backward and sees an image that seems to be behind the surface. A curved mirror changes the directions of rays and can make an image look larger or smaller.
facts: Many mirrors use a very thin coating of metal behind a flat piece of glass.

entries.title: Why pendulums swing back and forth
entries.answer: A pendulum is a weight hanging from a string or rod that can move side to side. If the weight is lifted and released, gravity pulls it toward the lowest point. It is still moving at the bottom, so it swings up the other side and then turns around again. With small swings, the time for a round trip depends mostly on the length. A clock can use nearly equal swings to count time.
facts: A longer pendulum swings more slowly than a shorter one under the same conditions.

entries.title: Why staying over your feet helps you balance
entries.answer: Imagine a straight line drawn downward from the place where your weight is balanced. When that line falls between your feet, your body can often stay steady. Lean far enough for it to go beyond your feet and you may have to take a step. Objects can tip for the same reason. A tall box with a heavy top is easier to tip than a box with the same weight packed near the bottom.
facts: Widening the space between your feet often makes balancing easier.

entries.title: Why steel ships can float
entries.answer: A steel nail sinks, but a ship made of steel can float because the hull takes up much more space than the steel alone. The wide hull keeps water out of air-filled spaces. When the ship sits in water, it pushes some water aside. The water pushes upward by the weight of the water moved out of its place. A floating ship settles until that upward push balances the weight of the whole ship and its cargo.
facts: A loaded ship floats lower because it needs to push more water aside.

entries.title: Why sunsets can turn red or orange
entries.answer: At sunset, the Sun is low on the horizon. Its light travels a longer, slanted path through the lower atmosphere than it did at midday. Along that path, much of the blue light is scattered away from the original beam. More red and orange light remains in the light reaching your eyes from near the Sun. Thin clouds can catch that reddish light after the ground is in shadow, so they sometimes glow even when daylight is fading.
facts: Sunrise can show similar colors for the same reason.
